passage: The clip reached Deepika's phone at 10 pm in her PG in Chandigarh: blurry footage of young men smashing a bus stop, captioned 'Students from THAT college did this today!! Share before it's deleted!!' Her floor group was already furious. Deepika, twenty-one, felt her own anger rise; that college had beaten hers in the debate finals. Then she noticed the capital letters, the rush, the 'before it's deleted.' She paused the clip. The shop signs were in a script she didn't recognise, and everyone wore winter coats, in May. She searched a still frame and found the same video from two years ago, in another country. She posted the link in the group. Gurleen replied, 'Okay, but they're still annoying.' Deepika laughed. 'Annoying, sure. Not criminals.'

qa.q: What did the caption tell people to do?
qa.a: Share it before it's deleted.

qa.q: Why did Deepika feel her anger rise at first?
qa.a: The clip targeted a college that had beaten hers in the debate finals, so it fed an existing grudge.

qa.q: Which clues helped Deepika spot that the clip was false?
qa.a: The shouting urgency of the caption, shop signs in an unfamiliar script and winter coats in May, which she then checked by searching a frame.

qa.q: How might students of the accused college be affected if the clip spread?
qa.a: They could be blamed and harassed for something they never did.

grounding: Shows a young adult noticing emotional manipulation in a viral clip and checking it before believing or sharing.

passage:
'Papa, that channel only interviews people who agree with them.'
'And your videos only show people who agree with you.'
Jagdish opened his mouth. Parul, his sister, looked up from her phone. 'He's got you there.'
'Fine. But the metro line will cut traffic by half.'
'Who said half?'
'The... video.'
'And who made the video?'
'...The company building it.' Jagdish rubbed his face. 'Okay. That's not neutral either.'
Papa softened. 'I'm not against the metro, beta. I'm against cutting the old trees in the market without asking anyone.'
'Wait, that's your whole objection?'
'That's what the channel never lets me say.'
Parul laughed. 'So you two agree more than your screens do.'
Jagdish opened the city council's report. 'Let's read the actual plan. Both of us. Tonight.'

qa.q: What is Papa's real objection to the metro line?
qa.a: Cutting the old trees in the market without asking anyone.

qa.q: What did Jagdish realise when he rubbed his face?
qa.a: He realised his own source was biased too, since it came from the company building the line.

qa.q: Why is reading the actual plan together a good next step?
qa.a: It moves them from competing slanted sources to the original document, and they check it together fairly.

qa.q: How does Parul see the argument?
qa.a: She sees that her father and brother agree more than they thought, and the screens made them seem further apart.

grounding: Illustrates a young adult recognising bias in his own sources and hearing an opposing view fairly.

passage: In the small back office of the travel agency where she had worked for three months, Avni, twenty-two, waited while her supervisor Mehak finished a call. Avni's part-time MBA exams fell on four Saturdays next month, and Saturday was their busiest day. She had rehearsed on the bus: ask, don't demand. 'Ma'am, I need those four Saturdays. I know it's peak. I can cover Sundays and two late shifts on Wednesdays, when the group bookings come in.' Mehak frowned. 'Sundays are dead. Wednesdays help, though.' 'Then three Wednesday late shifts?' Mehak tapped her pen. 'And you train the new intern on refunds before you go.' Avni hesitated; that was extra work. 'Done, if the training happens during my Wednesday shifts, not on top of them.' Mehak laughed. 'Fair. Write it down before either of us forgets.'

qa.q: How many Saturdays did Avni need off?
qa.a: Four Saturdays.

qa.q: Why did Avni hesitate before agreeing to train the intern?
qa.a: She saw it as extra work on top of what she had offered and wanted the deal to stay fair to her.

qa.q: What made Avni's approach to the request work?
qa.a: She came with specific offers instead of demands, listened to what Mehak valued, and protected her own interest with a small condition.

qa.q: How might Mehak see Avni after this conversation?
qa.a: As a reasonable, reliable employee who solves problems rather than just asking for favours.

grounding: Shows a young adult advocating for her needs at work and reaching a compromise that suits both sides.

passage:
Dear Bidisha Aunty,
Thank you for replying about the deposit. I understand you want to keep two months' rent for the marked wall and the broken geyser knob. I've been thinking about what's fair for both of us. The wall mark is from our shelf, and I'm sorry about it; I'm happy for the painting cost to come out of the deposit. The geyser knob, though, was already loose when we moved in; I've attached the photo I took on the first day, with the date. Could we split it this way: painting cost from the deposit, and the rest returned by the fifteenth? If you prefer, I can send a painter I know who charges less, and you can check the work.
Thank you for two good years here.
Sudha

qa.q: What did Sudha attach to the email?
qa.a: A dated photo of the loose geyser knob from her first day.

qa.q: What does Sudha's line about 'what's fair for both of us' show about her intention?
qa.a: She wants to protect her own money but also keep the relationship good, not win at the landlady's expense.

qa.q: What made Sudha's email persuasive?
qa.a: She admitted the damage that was hers, backed her other point with evidence, and offered a practical option.

qa.q: How might Bidisha Aunty read this email?
qa.a: She may feel respected rather than attacked, which makes her more likely to agree to the split.

grounding: Illustrates a young adult negotiating a deposit with her landlady, owning her part and proposing a fair compromise.

passage:
Monday: The offer letter from the Hyderabad firm arrived at 9 am. Lavanya, twenty-one, screamed and hugged her brother Manoj, then sat on her bed and felt her chest tighten. Her own flat. Her own salary. No one to call if the gas ran out.
Saturday: At the station, Amma packed pickle into three separate bags. Lavanya laughed at her, then cried in the train toilet for ten minutes, then took a selfie by the window, grinning. Both were true.
Two weeks later: She sent Manoj a photo of her tiny kitchen: 'Made rasam. It tastes wrong. I love it here. I miss everyone. Is that allowed?' He replied, 'Allowed. Send me the recipe you invented.'

qa.q: What did Amma pack into three separate bags?
qa.a: Pickle.

qa.q: What does Lavanya's message 'Is that allowed?' show about her feelings?
qa.a: She feels love for her new life and missing her family at once, and she is unsure if it's okay to feel both.

qa.q: How could Manoj keep supporting his sister from afar?
qa.a: He can keep reassuring her that mixed feelings are normal and stay in light, regular touch, like asking for her recipes.

qa.q: How might Amma have felt at the station?
qa.a: Proud and worried at once, which shows in her packing pickle into three bags.

grounding: Shows a young adult holding excitement about independence and fear or homesickness at the same time over several weeks.

passage: 'Sarika, you keep saying you should feel only happy about the scholarship,' said Swati Maasi, pouring tea. 'When I was twenty, I got a nursing seat in Delhi, the first girl from our village to leave for studies. The night before I left, I sat on the roof and couldn't decide if I was flying or falling. I wanted my own room, my own money, a city where nobody knew my business. And I was terrified. Of trains, of loneliness, of failing and coming back. My mother said, "Both feelings can sit on the same roof." I went. I cried every Sunday for three months. I also loved every Monday. You can say yes to something and still be scared of it, beta.'

qa.q: Where did Swati get her nursing seat?
qa.a: In Delhi.

qa.q: What did young Swati mean by 'flying or falling'?
qa.a: She felt excitement and fear at the same time and couldn't tell which was stronger.

qa.q: What might help Sarika with her own scholarship decision?
qa.a: Accepting that fear and excitement can live together, and deciding on what she wants rather than waiting for the fear to vanish.

qa.q: How might Swati's mother have felt about her daughter leaving?
qa.a: Probably proud and anxious too, yet she gave Swati permission to hold both feelings.

grounding: Illustrates an elder's memory of feeling both thrilled by independence and afraid of it as a young woman.

passage: 'Pooja, you asked why I keep driving past that old school,' said Samir, the senior engineer, as they waited at the signal. 'When I was twenty-one, in my final year, I went back there on a holiday. The guard let me in. The benches were so small. I sat on one and smelled chalk and the wet mud of the field, and suddenly I wanted to be ten again so badly it hurt. Back then someone packed my tiffin, someone else decided everything. I didn't have to choose a job or worry about my father's loan. I sat there for an hour. Then I walked out feeling strangely lighter. It was sweet and sad together. I still visit when life gets heavy.'

qa.q: What could young Samir smell sitting on the bench?
qa.a: Chalk and the wet mud of the field.

qa.q: What did Samir wish for as he sat on the small bench?
qa.a: He longed for the safety of being ten, when others made decisions and he had no adult worries.

qa.q: How could Pooja use Samir's story when adult life feels heavy?
qa.a: She could let herself revisit comforting memories briefly as a way to rest, and then return to her responsibilities.

qa.q: What would change if the guard hadn't let Samir in?
qa.a: He would have missed that moment of bittersweet comfort that still helps him today.

grounding: Shows a young adult's bittersweet longing for the simplicity and safety of childhood, told as a memory by a senior colleague.

passage: The truck was coming at six the next morning, and the old house in Bhopal had to be empty by then. Imran, nineteen, home from his hostel for just one day, was supposed to pack the storeroom. Rain drummed on the tin roof; the power kept flickering. He opened a trunk and found his old cricket bat, taped at the handle, with his name scratched in by Abba's knife. He sat down on the dusty floor holding it. His sister Swati found him there an hour later, nothing packed. 'Imran! We don't have time.' 'Remember when this whole yard was the world?' he said. She stopped. Then she sat beside him, just for five minutes, and neither of them spoke. After that they packed fast, and he put the bat in his own bag.

qa.q: When was the truck coming?
qa.a: At six the next morning.

qa.q: Why did Imran sit on the floor holding the bat instead of packing?
qa.a: It brought back the safe, simple world of his childhood in that house, and he felt a bittersweet longing he couldn't rush past.

qa.q: What did Swati get right despite the time pressure?
qa.a: She paused and sat with him briefly, honouring the feeling, and then they packed quickly together.

qa.q: How might Swati have felt when she first found him with nothing packed?
qa.a: Frustrated and stressed about the deadline, until his words pulled her into the memory too.

grounding: Illustrates a young adult's bittersweet longing for childhood while emptying the family home against a deadline.

passage: The night before his first day at the design studio in Gurugram, Baljeet, twenty-two, couldn't stop moving. He ironed his shirt twice, repacked his bag three times, and texted his friend Darshan a photo of his new ID card. They met at the tea stall near his PG at ten. 'You're vibrating,' Darshan said. 'I'll get my own desk, yaar. My own projects. First salary, I'm taking Mummy to the hills.' He talked about buying a secondhand scooter, about evening classes in animation, about one day starting his own studio. Darshan grinned and let him go on. Walking back, Baljeet looked up at the half-built towers against the orange sky and thought that, for once, the future looked like something he was walking toward, not waiting for.

qa.q: Where is the design studio?
qa.a: In Gurugram.

qa.q: What does Baljeet ironing his shirt twice suggest about his mood?
qa.a: It suggests he felt eager and restless with excitement about starting his first job.

qa.q: How could Baljeet use this energy well once he starts?
qa.a: He could turn it into steady effort in the first weeks and pick one plan, like the animation classes, to begin.

qa.q: How does Darshan respond to Baljeet's excitement?
qa.a: He is amused and supportive, grinning and letting Baljeet talk without dampening his hopes. 🙂

grounding: Shows a young adult's forward-looking eagerness the night before his first job.

passage:
'Tushar, look. The hostel faces the sea.'
'You've shown me that photo nine times.'
'Ten. And the lab has a boat. An actual boat.'
Their mother called from the kitchen, 'Has she stopped talking about fish?'
'Never,' Lakshmi called back. 'Amma, I'll be diving by second year.'
'After your swimming improves.'
'It will. I've already asked the pool here for morning slots.' She spread the brochure on the bed. 'And there's an internship with turtle nests. And I'll learn Konkani. And...'
Tushar laughed. 'Breathe.'
'I can't. It's like my life finally has a door and I'm standing right in front of it.'
He was quiet a moment. 'I'm going to miss you, you know.'
Lakshmi hugged the brochure. 'Visit. I'll show you the boat.'

qa.q: What does Lakshmi's hostel face?
qa.a: The sea.

qa.q: What did Lakshmi mean by 'my life finally has a door'?
qa.a: She feels her adult life opening up with real possibilities and is eager to step into it.

qa.q: What shows Lakshmi turning excitement into action?
qa.a: She has already asked the local pool for morning slots to improve her swimming.

qa.q: How does Tushar feel about his sister's excitement?
qa.a: He is amused and teasing, but also sad that he will miss her when she leaves.

grounding: Illustrates a young adult's eager, forward-looking energy about a new course and adult life.

passage: At the bank branch, Binita, twenty-two, sat holding a folder of forms: new salary account, tax declaration, nominee details, and the rent agreement her landlord wanted notarised by Friday. Two weeks ago she had been a student whose biggest worry was a viva. Now the clerk, Noor, was asking for a cancelled cheque, and Binita realised she didn't have a chequebook and couldn't remember whether her ID proof was the original or a copy. Her eyes stung. She stared at the forms and couldn't read a single line. 'Are you okay, beta?' Noor asked. 'I don't know where to start,' Binita whispered. Noor took the folder and made three piles. 'Today, only this one. The others can wait till Monday.' Binita breathed out for what felt like the first time that morning.

qa.q: By when did the landlord want the rent agreement notarised?
qa.a: By Friday.

qa.q: Why couldn't Binita read a single line of the forms?
qa.a: She felt flooded by so many new adult tasks at once that her mind froze.

qa.q: Why did Noor's three piles help?
qa.a: They broke a flood of tasks into one manageable step for today, which unfroze Binita.

qa.q: How might Noor have seen Binita's situation?
qa.a: As a young person facing many adult tasks for the first time, which she met with patience rather than irritation.

grounding: Shows a young adult frozen by a sudden pile of permanent adult responsibilities, and being helped to take one step.

passage:
Dear Tejas Bhaiya,
Sorry I didn't reply for two weeks. Since Papa's transfer, it's been me at home with Dadi, plus the new job, plus the electricity bill, the gas booking, Dadi's appointments, the house help's salary. Every morning I wake up and the list is just there, sitting on my chest. Yesterday I stood in the kitchen for twenty minutes holding the gas booking slip, not doing anything, and then cried because the milk boiled over. I know people do this every day. I just didn't know it all arrives at once and never leaves. I'm writing because you said to tell you if it got too much. It's too much, a bit. Can we talk on Sunday? I'll make a list of what I actually need help with.
Mehak

qa.q: How long did Mehak stand in the kitchen holding the gas booking slip?
qa.a: Twenty minutes.

qa.q: What does Mehak mean by the list 'sitting on my chest'?
qa.a: She feels weighed down and anxious from the moment she wakes by all the new responsibilities.

qa.q: What makes Mehak's plan to talk on Sunday a good step?
qa.a: She is reaching out instead of hiding it, and planning to name specific needs so the help can be practical.

qa.q: How might Tejas feel reading this letter?
qa.a: Concerned for her, but glad she trusted him and told him, as he had asked. 🤍

grounding: Illustrates a young adult paralysed by a sudden load of household and work responsibilities, and reaching out.

passage: I'm Omkar, Maria's younger brother. Last month her engagement to the man she'd been with since college ended. Five years. She didn't explain much to us, only that it was over and nobody did anything terrible. At first she kept going to work like normal. Then I noticed she'd stopped singing in the shower, which she has done my whole life. On Sunday she sat on the balcony with the box of wedding cards they had already printed and folded them into little boats, one by one, without speaking. I sat with her. I don't know if she was angry or just very sad. When the box was empty, she said, 'I had the whole house planned. Even the curtains.' Then she went in and made us both tea.

qa.q: How long had Maria been with the man?
qa.a: Five years, since college.

qa.q: What might folding the wedding cards into boats suggest about Maria's feelings?
qa.a: It may suggest she was quietly grieving the future she had planned and letting it go slowly, though Omkar can't be sure.

qa.q: How could Omkar keep supporting his sister?
qa.a: He can keep sitting with her without pushing for explanations, and if the sadness stays heavy, gently suggest family time or a counsellor.

qa.q: How might this loss feel different for Maria than for her family?
qa.a: For her it is the loss of a whole imagined life, down to the curtains; the family sees the breakup but not all the plans that ended with it.

grounding: Shows a young adult grieving the end of a long relationship and the future she had imagined, seen by her brother.

passage:
Week one: The doctor's words were gentle, but Jomon, twenty-one, heard only that he would never play at that level again. At home he turned his team jersey inside out and stuffed it at the back of the cupboard. When Ishita called, he said he was fine and hung up.
Week three: Ishita came anyway, with banana chips. He talked for an hour about the trials he'd miss, the coach who had believed in him, the future he had drawn since he was twelve. He cried, which he hadn't done in years. She just listened.
Week six: He went to the ground as a spectator for the first time. It hurt to watch. On the way out he asked the junior coach if they needed help with the under-twelves.

qa.q: What did Jomon do with his team jersey?
qa.a: He turned it inside out and stuffed it at the back of the cupboard.

qa.q: Why did Jomon tell Ishita he was fine and hang up in week one?
qa.a: He was too raw with grief to talk and wanted to shut out the loss of his future.

qa.q: What helped Jomon move from hiding to grieving?
qa.a: Ishita coming anyway and listening without trying to fix things gave him space to cry and talk.

qa.q: How might the under-twelves be affected if Jomon helps coach?
qa.a: They would gain a skilled, dedicated coach who knows the game deeply.

grounding: Illustrates a young adult processing the loss of an idealised sporting future over several weeks.

passage: The placement cell office smelled of printer ink. Aparna Ma'am turned the screen toward Simran, twenty-one. 'The company has frozen hiring this year. It's not about your interview.' For a moment Simran wanted to argue, to ask if she could call them, write to someone, reapply. She had planned the last two years around this job. Instead she looked out of the window at the rain for a while. 'So that door's closed.' 'For now, yes.' Simran nodded slowly. 'Then what's still open?' Aparna Ma'am pulled out a list: two smaller firms, a research assistant post, a one-year diploma. Simran took a photo of it. Her hands were steady, though her throat was tight. 'I'll come back on Thursday with the ones I want.'

qa.q: Why did the company not hire this year?
qa.a: It had frozen hiring.

qa.q: What does Simran's tight throat alongside steady hands suggest?
qa.a: She was still sad about losing the job she had planned for, yet calm enough to accept it and move forward.

qa.q: Which choice helped Simran most in that moment?
qa.a: Asking what was still open instead of fighting a decision she couldn't change.

qa.q: How might Aparna Ma'am feel seeing Simran's response?
qa.a: Relieved and encouraged, since helping a student plan next steps is easier than managing a fight against a closed door.

grounding: Shows a young adult accepting a disappointing, unchangeable outcome and turning to what is still possible.

passage:
Dear Kishore,
You asked how I'm handling the shop closing. Honestly, for months I fought it. I made spreadsheets, talked to lenders, stayed up planning how to save Papa's electronics shop, even though Papa himself had already decided. Online sellers, rising rent, his back pain; it just doesn't add up anymore. Last Sunday I helped him pull the shutter down for the last time. I expected to feel crushed. Instead I mostly felt tired, and then oddly quiet. Papa put his hand on the shutter and said, 'Thirty years. Good years.' I realised I was fighting something he had already made peace with. I'm not happy about it. But I've stopped arguing with it. Next month I'll help him set up a small repair corner at home.
Kunal

qa.q: How long had the shop run?
qa.a: Thirty years.

qa.q: What did Kunal realise when Papa touched the shutter?
qa.a: That he had been fighting a change his father had already made peace with, which helped him stop resisting.

qa.q: What does Kunal's plan for a home repair corner show about his next step?
qa.a: He has moved from resisting the loss to adapting, finding a new way forward that fits the new reality.

qa.q: How might Papa have felt about Kunal's months of trying to save the shop?
qa.a: Perhaps touched by his son's effort, but also tired, since he had already accepted the closing.

grounding: Illustrates a young adult moving from fighting a family business closure to accepting it and adapting.

passage: Javier, twenty-one, read the results on the board outside the training centre in Valencia twice before it sank in: failed again, the second time, by four points. He walked out and sat on the curb in the heat. His friend Chen, who had passed, sat down beside him without saying anything about his own result. 'I'm done,' Javier said. 'My uncle was right. I should just keep stacking boxes at the warehouse.' Chen waited. After a while Javier pulled the marked paper from his bag and looked at it properly. Almost all his mistakes were in the circuit calculations, not the practical. 'It's always the same section,' he muttered. That evening he taped the paper above his bed and asked Chen for his old calculation notes. The next exam was in March. He wrote the date on his hand.

qa.q: By how many points did Javier fail?
qa.a: Four points.

qa.q: Why did Javier say 'I'm done' at first?
qa.a: He felt crushed and discouraged after failing twice and was echoing his uncle's doubts.

qa.q: What turned Javier's setback into a plan?
qa.a: Looking closely at the marked paper showed his mistakes were in one section, which gave him a clear target to study.

qa.q: Why might Chen have said nothing about his own result?
qa.a: He sensed Javier's pain and chose to support him quietly rather than highlight his own pass.

grounding: Shows a young adult finding the grit to try again after a second failed exam.

passage: At the district sports hostel, the track lights came on at six. Sangeeta, twenty, had missed selection for the state relay team by one-tenth of a second, two weeks after coming back from a hamstring injury. For three days she didn't come to practice. On the fourth, Coach Manjula found her sitting in the stands. 'You can quit,' the coach said evenly. 'Nobody will blame you.' Sangeeta was quiet for a long time. 'If I quit now, the injury decides. I want to decide.' She laced her spikes. The first two starts were ugly; her leg felt stiff and her face burned with embarrassment in front of the juniors. On the third, she found her rhythm again. Coach Manjula wrote the next trial date on the whiteboard and underlined it twice.

qa.q: By how much did Sangeeta miss selection?
qa.a: By one-tenth of a second.

qa.q: What did Sangeeta mean by 'I want to decide'?
qa.a: She didn't want the injury and setback to end her running for her; she wanted to choose to keep trying.

qa.q: What was wise about the coach saying 'You can quit'?
qa.a: It removed pressure and let Sangeeta find her own reason to continue, which makes her determination stronger.

qa.q: How might the juniors see Sangeeta's ugly starts?
qa.a: They might notice her struggling, but also learn that senior athletes keep going after setbacks.

grounding: Illustrates a young athlete building the resolve to return to training after a painful setback.

passage: By the third week of the product launch, the office on the ninth floor had gone silent except for keyboards. Sachin, twenty-two, had been eating lunch at his desk and dreaming about spreadsheets. On Friday his colleague Yash dragged an old carrom board out of the storeroom and set it on the pantry table. 'Fifteen minutes. One game. Loser buys chai.' Sachin said he had a report due. Yash flicked the striker toward him. Sachin sighed, sat down, and missed three easy shots in a row. Yash did a dramatic slow-motion celebration. Sachin laughed so hard he snorted, which set off the two interns watching. He lost, bought the chai, and went back to his desk. The report took him half the time he had expected.

qa.q: Where did Yash find the carrom board?
qa.a: In the storeroom.

qa.q: Why did Sachin say he had a report due?
qa.a: He felt so pressured by work that he believed he couldn't spare even fifteen minutes to play.

qa.q: What could Sachin and Yash do to keep this balance going?
qa.a: They could make the Friday game a short regular ritual, so play is part of the week rather than a rare break.

qa.q: How might the interns watching experience this moment?
qa.a: They would see their colleagues laughing, which could ease their own stress and make the office feel friendlier. 😊

grounding: Shows young adults using a short game and laughter to counter work stress during a busy launch.

passage:
Dear Mridul,
Remember the silly comic strips we used to draw in the back of our physics notebooks? The one about the angry pressure cooker? I found them while moving flats last week, and I laughed so loudly my new neighbour knocked to check on me. It made me realise I haven't done anything just for fun in about a year. It's been job, commute, sleep, repeat, and I've been snapping at everyone. So I bought a cheap sketchbook, and every night now I draw one silly panel before bed. Last night it was my boss as a sleepy owl. No one will ever see it. My shoulders have come down from my ears a bit. Shall we restart the strip? You do the words, I'll draw, like old times. 🙂
Sumit

qa.q: What did Sumit find while moving flats?
qa.a: The old comic strips from their physics notebooks.

qa.q: What did Sumit realise after laughing at the old comics?
qa.a: He realised he hadn't done anything just for fun in about a year and that work had squeezed out play.

qa.q: Why is one silly panel a night a good habit for Sumit?
qa.a: It is small enough to keep up daily, and it gives him regular lightness that eases his stress.

qa.q: How might Mridul feel receiving this letter?
qa.a: Probably amused and happy to be remembered, and tempted to restart the strip together.

grounding: Illustrates a young adult bringing back a playful hobby as a counterweight to work stress.
